step1_summary.Chief complaint: Dysuria (painful urination) and urinary frequency for just under a week.
Symptoms: Aching pain in lower abdomen worsened by urination
Pink discoloration of urine (possible hematuria) noted today
No fever, nausea, vomiting, or back/flank pain
Medications/Allergies: Medication for IBS (name uncertain, possibly for cramp relief)
Family/Social history: No family history of bladder or kidney problems or other relevant issues
Lives in university halls with flatmate
First time smoked weed 1.5 weeks ago
Sexually active with boyfriend; uses combined pill, no consistent condom use
step1_summary.Vital signs/Exam findings: Not explicitly mentioned, but patient denies fever or systemic signs; clinician did not find exam concerning.
step1_summary.Labs/Imaging: Urine sample planned for microscopy and culture; no results yet.

V: Urinary tract vessel injury or hemorrhage: Pink urine could be from bleeding due to inflammation or trauma.
Renal/ureteral stone with microhematuria: Could cause pain and hematuria though no flank pain reported.
I: Urinary tract infection (cystitis): Classic symptoms of dysuria, frequency, lower abdominal discomfort, and hematuria.
Urethritis (possibly sexually transmitted infection): Despite no discharge, unprotected sex increases risk.
N: Bladder tumor or polyp: Rare at this age but can cause hematuria and dysuria.
Urethral neoplasm: Very unlikely given short duration and age.
D: IBS-related bladder irritation: Overlap possible but IBS usually does not cause hematuria or burning urination.
Vitamin C excess leading to urinary symptoms (unlikely here).
I2: Antibiotic side effect or allergic reaction causing urinary symptoms (patient currently not on antibiotics).
C: Congenital urinary tract abnormalities causing recurrent infections (no history supporting this).
A: Allergic/interstitial cystitis: Chronic bladder inflammation, often without infection.
Autoimmune cystitis: Less likely given acute presentation.
T: Trauma to urinary tract: No history of trauma reported.
Sexual activity-related trauma or irritation: Possible but no reported injuries.
E: Diabetes mellitus causing increased frequency and UTI susceptibility (no symptoms suggesting hyperglycemia).

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic presentation with dysuria, frequency, lower abdominal pain worsened by urination, and recent hematuria. No systemic symptoms to suggest complicated infection.
supporting_evidence: Burning pain on urination and frequency for less than a week
Lower abdominal aching pain associated with urination
Pink discoloration of urine indicating possible hematuria
Denial of systemic symptoms (fever or flank pain) consistent with uncomplicated UTI
opposing_evidence: No fever or systemic signs (though not mandatory for UTI)
No vaginal discharge (less likely STI but not excluded)

opposing_evidence: No abnormal vaginal or urethral discharge
